hero.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
hero.body:
A Jensen Beach teenager will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend, following years of competitive sailing that started when she was four years old. Harper Aberman first discovered the sport at a summer camp in Pennsylvania that her grandparents enrolled her in. "They then decided to throw my cousin and me into summer camp, where they then did a four-week course, and my cousin hated it, and I fell in love with it, and I ended up going for eight weeks," Aberman said.

When her family relocated to Jensen Beach, Aberman joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive sailing career truly began to flourish. "That is where the sailing adventure took off for me," Aberman said. Aberman describes herself as an adrenaline junkie and says she is drawn to the sport's most challenging conditions. "When it's windy, I've always struggled to stay upright and stay out of the water," she said. Despite her modest self-assessment, Aberman has won countless tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and established herself as one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit.

Aberman learned she would represent Team USA during Spring Break when she received the life-changing email. "It was during Spring Break, I got the email. I started screaming, my parents started screaming, and we were like, 'This is not real. We're going to Europe this summer," Aberman said. To prepare for the championship, she has spent recent weeks training in Spain ahead of the competition.

Racing begins Monday at the venue in France. Aberman explained the training demands the location has required. "We plan on taking the waters Monday for racing, and it's just been a lot of recovery and a lot of time and effort out on the water, but it's definitely going to be worth it. Especially in the venue we're in," she said. The championship represents a significant milestone for the competitive sailor who developed her passion for the sport at the US Sailing Center of Martin County.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County homeowners face thousands in surprise sewer bills from Delray Beach audit
cards.body:
Residents in an unincorporated Palm Beach County neighborhood are grappling with unexpected retroactive sewer bills from the city of Delray Beach, with some bills exceeding $4,000. Homeowners along Franwood Drive received notices demanding payment for years of unpaid sewer fees following a city audit completed in April 2026. The bills cover up to three years of charges at $90 per month, plus new monthly sewer fees going forward. Candace Etzler received a notice for $3,139, while her neighbor Ruth Stephens faces a bill totaling $4,494.92. At least a dozen homeowners in the area received similar notices.

The root of the issue traces back to 1998, when development in the area disrupted the residents' septic systems. State law required them to connect to the nearest municipal sewer system as a result. However, residents say they attempted to pay for sewer service in the past but were told they did not need to do so. The city's recent audit triggered the retroactive billing, catching residents off guard. "We were in total shock because it feels like we're being punished," Stephens said. Etzler added her frustration about the calculation method, saying "How can you have this random number of 36 months and at the price of $90 a month."

City Commissioner Juli Casale defended the billing decision in a statement, explaining that the city must determine costs incurred and recover applicable fees from those receiving service. "This is about ensuring that public utility costs are paid by those receiving the service rather than being shifted to the taxpayers," Casale said. Despite this rationale, residents question both how the back charges were calculated and the fairness of being billed retroactively without warning. Some homeowners have already paid the fees or enrolled in payment plans out of fear their service could be disconnected.

County Commissioner Marci Woodward has begun investigating the matter, stating she is working with the county attorney to examine the legality of the retroactive charges and the ongoing monthly payments. Residents acknowledge they understand the need to pay monthly sewer fees but argue the thousands in back charges are unreasonable given the circumstances. The situation reflects growing tension between municipal cost recovery and resident concerns about fairness and transparency in utility billing practices.

cards.headline: New Florida law opens $167 million for mobile home repairs and storm hardening
cards.teaser: Senate Bill 594 expands state SHIP funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm retrofits, with applications opening in August.
cards.body:
Senate Bill 594 took effect July 1 and opens $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The law followed an investigation that found nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida, about two-thirds of the state's more than 1 million such homes, were built before current federal safety standards, leaving them unable to withstand modern storms. The investigation was prompted by an EF-3 tornado that destroyed 138 homes at Spanish Lakes Country Club Community in Fort Pierce and killed six residents.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services said an online portal will open in August. Once it launches, about 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law and plans to offer lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance for manufactured home owners. St. Lucie County is waiting on final state guidance before announcing its application process. Indian River County plans to take the item to the Board on August 18, with a September 30 deadline to submit its plan to the state. Stellatos said funding is first come, first served.

cards.headline: Fourth of July holiday sees surge in deadly car crashes with impaired driving rates higher than typical
cards.teaser: Last Fourth of July, 579 people died in car crashes nationwide, with nearly 4 in 10 deaths involving impaired driving, significantly higher than the typical 30 percent rate seen throughout the year.
cards.body:
The Fourth of July ranks as one of America's most dangerous holidays for drivers. Last Fourth of July, 579 people died in car crashes nationwide, with deadly crashes spiking 44 percent on Independence Day. Nearly 4 in 10 of those deaths involved impaired driving, significantly higher than the typical 30 percent rate seen throughout the year. Teenagers make up about 10 percent of these holiday fatalities, according to federal statistics.

Rideshare apps like Uber and Lyft are experiencing surge demand as celebrants use them as their designated drivers. Local safety campaigns encourage everyone to plan ahead using rideshares, taxis, or public transportation. Local residents in downtown West Palm Beach are heeding the message. "I will be paddle boarding, but I will have a designated truck driver drop us off and pick us up," Scott said. "I'm gonna take an Uber to come celebrate," Pamela explained about her July 4th plans. To save money on rides, leave early or wait out peak hours to avoid surge pricing, walk a few blocks away from crowded areas for easier pickup, and compare prices across different rideshare apps.

cards.headline: Manufactured home owners can apply for Florida's $167 million repair funding starting in August
cards.teaser: Nearly 140 new Florida laws took effect Wednesday, including one that could be a game-changer for some of the state's most vulnerable homeowners. Senate Bill 594 opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits.
cards.body:
Nearly 140 new Florida laws took effect in July, including Senate Bill 594, which opens $167 million in state affordable housing funding to manufactured and mobile home owners. The law allows residents to use these funds for emergency repairs, lot rent assistance, and storm-hardening retrofits. The change came after an investigation revealed a critical vulnerability in Florida's housing stock: nearly 700,000 homes, representing about two-thirds of the state's more than 1 million mobile and manufactured homes, were built before current federal safety standards and cannot withstand modern storms. Many seniors living in these older homes cannot afford to make the necessary improvements to protect themselves and their families.

The investigation was sparked by an EF-3 tornado that destroyed homes at Spanish Lakes Country Club in Fort Pierce, killing six residents and destroying 138 homes. Homeowners across Florida subsequently pleaded with lawmakers for assistance, leading to the passage and implementation of Senate Bill 594. Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services explained that an online portal will open in August for eligible applicants. About 75 percent of Martin County's annual SHIP funding, which typically ranges from $1 million to $1.5 million, could now support mobile and manufactured homeowners. Residents can complete applications online or request that the office mail them a copy.

The five-county region is preparing to launch the program with varying timelines. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law and plans to offer lot rent, rehabilitation, and emergency repair assistance once the program opens. St. Lucie County is awaiting final guidance from the state before announcing its application process. Indian River County officials scheduled a Board meeting for August 18th to address the legislative change, with a September 30th deadline to submit their implementation plan to the state. According to Stellatos, while counties follow a general calendar from the Florida Housing Coalition, the specific timing varies by location.

People interested in applying should visit the Florida Housing Finance Corporation website and select their county or city to learn about available funding, check income eligibility requirements, find contact information, and understand the application process. Stellatos emphasized that funding is distributed on a first-come, first-served basis, so applicants should gather their paperwork immediately to be ready when applications open in their area. She noted that the new law addresses a long-standing gap, finally providing assistance to residents who previously had no access to these resources.

The change follows an investigation that exposed nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida built before current federal safety standards, leaving them unable to withstand modern storms. The investigation was prompted by an EF-3 tornado that destroyed 138 homes at Spanish Lakes Country Club Community in Fort Pierce, killing six residents.

Martin County Human Services will open an online application portal in August for eligible manufactured home owners to access state housing funds. About 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, will now help mobile and manufactured homeowners under the new law. cards.headline: Florida law requiring heart screenings for high school athletes takes effect statewide
cards.body:
A new Florida law mandating heart screenings for high school student athletes went into effect July 1, fulfilling a commitment born from tragedy in Port St. Joe. The Second Chance Act requires all high school student athletes to receive a medical evaluation that includes an electrocardiogram, commonly known as an EKG, before participating in school-sanctioned sports. The legislation, HB 1135, was sponsored by Rep. Jason Shoaf in the House and carried by Sen. Corey Simon in the Senate during the 2025 Legislative Session. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the measure last summer. The law honors Chance Gainer, a standout athlete at Port St. Joe High School who collapsed and died from sudden cardiac arrest during a rivalry football game.

Sudden cardiac arrest represents the leading cause of death among student athletes, accounting for approximately 75 percent of all student athlete deaths. According to research, roughly 1 in every 300 students may have an undiagnosed heart condition with the potential to be life-threatening. For 80 percent of these students, cardiac arrest serves as the first symptom. Implementing EKG screenings allows medical professionals to identify these conditions before they become fatal. Chance Gainer's parents, Equila and JJ, channeled their grief into advocating for the law's passage. "Today marks more than just the start of a new law, it marks a promise kept," Shoaf said, emphasizing that the legislation represents "a promise to every parent in Florida that we will do our best to protect their children."

PanCare of Florida has partnered with Who We Play For to provide free sports physicals and heart screenings to student athletes throughout the region. Evan Ernst, Founder and CEO of Who We Play For, stressed the importance of the measure. "The Second Chance Act represents the state-wide commitment we need to make these heart screenings accessible to every student athlete in our state," Ernst said. He added that the organization operates under the principle that no family should experience the tragedies the Gainer family endured, particularly when such outcomes could be prevented through proper precautionary measures.

As fall practice seasons approach, families should prioritize scheduling their child's required sports physical immediately. Information regarding free EKG screening events is available through the partnering organizations. The law's implementation ensures that student athletes across Florida will have access to potentially lifesaving cardiac evaluations before they compete in school-sanctioned sports.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach secures $2 million for Australian Avenue flood repairs after years of street flooding
cards.teaser: Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street could finally see drainage improvements after the state allocated $2 million in the new Florida budget, though the project's full cost is estimated at $65 million.
cards.body:
The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue in West Palm Beach, a roadway neighbors say has flooded for as long as they can remember. State Sen. Mack Bernard secured the funding after Gov. DeSantis vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. The project targets Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street. Residents describe water pushing into driveways and leaving debris scattered across properties after even light storms. Marion Hawkins, who lives near the roadway, calls it "Lake Australian Avenue" because rainwater comes all the way up to her driveway and yard.

Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, has been riding his bike through flooded streets since childhood. The $2 million in state funding covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost. Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented plans three years ago that included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to make room for larger underground drainage pipes. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled to run through 2029.

cards.headline: Palm Beach International Airport begins transition to Donald J. Trump International Airport with July 9 official date
cards.teaser: Palm Beach International Airport is changing its name to Donald J. Trump International Airport on July 9, with signs already being swapped out as part of a state-funded $2.75 million transition.
cards.body:
Palm Beach International Airport is transitioning to Donald J. Trump International Airport, with the official name change taking effect July 9. Signs are already being swapped out as part of a transition funded by the state of Florida at a cost of $2.75 million. The official three-letter designation will change from PBI to DJT, used for airline reservations and navigation purposes, in August. The airport remains owned by Palm Beach County, while Trump owns the trademark on the new name. Airport officials said nothing should change for passengers beyond the signage.

The airport posted a statement on its website acknowledging the transition: "While we recognize that the required name change may be received in different ways by our passengers, we're grateful for your continued support through this transition period." Two lawsuits are attempting to stop the name change. George Poncy, one of the plaintiffs suing to block it, said the state appears to be stalling and delaying any hearing before a judge, with the possibility the case could be scheduled after the name change takes effect.

cards.headline: Martin County free clinic sees more patients after ACA subsidies expired, says it has room for more
cards.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County reports only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, but estimates show upwards of 500 people in the county may have lost access to health insurance.
cards.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free medical clinic in Martin County serving low-income families, is seeing more patients after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year. Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of the clinic, said more than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year. While only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access to health insurance.

Rokaya McGarry is one of those patients. She said she could no longer afford health insurance after the enhanced ACA subsidies expired and began to see medical care as a luxury until she fell very ill after losing her mother. She called the clinic and within a day Volunteers in Medicine took over her care. To qualify for care at the clinic, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. Bromberg said there are many more people out there who can come to the clinic, and the clinic has the capacity for more patients.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Marine deputies rescue two boaters after vessel sinks in Intracoastal Waterway
cards.teaser: Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on Tuesday, thanks to a quick response from marine deputies and the life-saving decisi.
cards.body:
Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on July 1, thanks to a quick response from marine deputies and the life-saving decision to wear life jackets. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit responded to reports of a small motorized boat taking on water and becoming submerged. Both occupants ended up in the water when their boat went down, but deputies say they were wearing life jackets that kept them afloat while help arrived. Body-worn camera footage captured the rescue as it unfolded.

Marine Unit deputies quickly located the pair in the water and safely brought them aboard their patrol vessel. The boaters were then transported back to the boat ramp without any injuries reported. "This incident serves as an important reminder that wearing a life jacket can save your life," the sheriff's office said in a Facebook post. "We're grateful this call ended safely and proud of the swift response by our Marine Unit deputies who are always ready to answer the call."

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes
cards.teaser: Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira, killing her 17-year-old cousin, grandmother, uncle and his wife.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering if her parents survived two devastating earthquakes that struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week. Her best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, woke De La Correa with nonstop phone calls in the middle of the night after the earthquake struck. Her parents survived, but several relatives did not. De La Correa lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife. The losses came just weeks after De La Correa returned from her first visit to Venezuela in several years, when she traveled there to announce she and her partner are expecting a baby later this year. The family gathered together for Mother's Day during her final weekend in the country. Claudia, who had planned to study dentistry after high school, was rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed.

The earthquake also destroyed De La Correa's parents' home and businesses. Her mother's children's clothing store was located inside a shopping mall that collapsed entirely. Feeling powerless from abroad, Carla Alvarado launched a GoFundMe campaign to support De La Correa's relatives. The campaign aims to raise $15,000 and is quickly spreading. De La Correa said the support from friends and strangers has become a lifeline as her parents search the ruins of their apartment building for salvageable belongings, recovering some clothing, photos and documents.

cards.teaser: Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on Tuesday, thanks to a quick response from marine deputies and the life-saving decision to wear life jackets.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit responded to reports of a small motorized boat taking on water and becoming submerged in the Intracoastal Waterway on July 1. Body-worn camera footage captured the rescue as it unfolded. Both occupants ended up in the water when their boat went down, but deputies say they were wearing life jackets that kept them afloat while help arrived.

Marine Unit deputies quickly located the pair in the water and safely brought them aboard their patrol vessel. The boaters were then transported back to the boat ramp without any injuries reported. "This incident serves as an important reminder that wearing a life jacket can save your life," the sheriff's office said in a Facebook post. "We're grateful this call ended safely and proud of the swift response by our Marine Unit deputies who are always ready to answer the call."

cards.headline: West Palm Beach gets $2 million state funding for Australian Avenue flood repairs
cards.teaser: Storm-weary drivers and residents along one of West Palm Beach's most flood-prone roads could finally see relief after years of dealing with rising water every .
cards.body:
Storm-weary drivers and residents along one of West Palm Beach's most flood-prone roads could finally see relief after years of dealing with rising water during routine rainfall. The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a long-discussed drainage project along Australian Avenue, a roadway neighbors say has flooded for as long as they can remember. The project targets Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street, an area Palm Beach County leaders have identified as needing major drainage improvements. State Sen. Mack Bernard secured the funding after Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. The $2 million covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost.

Residents have described the flooding's impact on their daily lives. Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, said flooding has affected his routine for years, forcing him to navigate through flooded streets during his commute. Marion Hawkins, who lives near the roadway, calls it "Lake Australian Avenue." She said rainwater comes all the way up to her driveway and yard, leaving debris scattered across her property. Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented improvement plans three years ago, which included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to make room for larger underground drainage pipes. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled through 2029.

cards.headline: Benjamin Franklin artifact collection goes on display at Historical Society of Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will be on display at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach starting next week. Zachary Jacobson of Palm Beach Gardens owns the collection with his brother.
cards.body:
One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will be on display at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach starting July 6 through August. The exhibit, titled Benjamin Franklin: Creating an American Icon, is owned by Zachary Jacobson of Palm Beach Gardens and his brother, who are displaying it to celebrate America's 250th birthday. The collection features over 50 books written by, printed by or about Franklin, along with work from his time as a printer. Artwork of the founding father covers the walls, including an original portrait. Among the standout pieces are a grandfather clock originally from Franklin's home in Philadelphia, a plate inscribed "B. Franklin," and original medallions made when Franklin was representing France during the American Revolution.

More than 120 pieces are on display, covering the full scope of Franklin's roles as statesman, printer and inventor. Jacobson's stepfather started the collection 50 years ago, and the brothers eventually bought the remains and continued it for 15 years. Notable items include a copy of Experiments and Observations on Electricity Made at Philadelphia owned by Franklin's son William, a tall-case tidal clock kept in Franklin's Philadelphia home, and the glass armonica, which Franklin called his favorite invention. The exhibit is free to the public and located at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County at 300 N Dixie Hwy.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
cards.teaser: A Jensen Beach teenager is set to represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend after years of competitive sailing.
cards.body:
Harper Aberman started sailing at age four at a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania that her grandparents enrolled her in. After her family moved to Jensen Beach, Aberman joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive career took shape. Aberman has won countless tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and is considered one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit.

Aberman received the news that she would represent Team USA during Spring Break via email. She has spent the past few weeks training in Spain ahead of the Sailing World Championship in France. Racing is set to begin Monday.

cards.headline: One year later: Alligator Alcatraz detention facility opened, closed and left questions unanswered
cards.teaser: One year ago, Florida opened a detention facility in the middle of the Everglades that would become one of the most controversial immigration detention camps in the country. Before July 1, 2025, no state had ever run a detention facility exclusively for immigration detainees.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced the opening of Alligator Alcatraz alongside Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on July 1, 2025. Trump described the facility as a place to house what he called the most dangerous migrants in the country. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old landing strip belonging to Miami-Dade County, then used emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management to build the facility in eight days. Trump said the Federal Emergency Management Agency would pay for Alligator Alcatraz. Using ICE's own data, investigations uncovered that about 70 percent of detainees there had no criminal record, debunking government claims that only criminals would be sent there. Immigration attorneys raised alarms about conditions inside. The American Civil Liberties Union led a federal lawsuit over detainees' access to legal counsel, asserting attorneys could not show up without an appointment and that clients were unable to place unmonitored outgoing calls to their attorneys.

Friends of the Everglades, led by Director Eve Samples, joined forces with the Miccosukee Tribe and other environmental groups to file a separate federal lawsuit claiming the construction violated the National Environmental Policy Act. News broke in May that Alligator Alcatraz would soon close. On June 16, ICE confirmed that all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through Alligator Alcatraz. Most estimates put the total price tag at more than one billion dollars. The ACLU and Friends of the Everglades lawsuits are still active.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
hero.body:
A Jensen Beach teenager will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend, following years of competitive sailing that started when she was four years old. Harper Aberman first discovered the sport at a summer camp in Pennsylvania that her grandparents enrolled her in. "They then decided to throw my cousin and me into summer camp, where they then did a four-week course, and my cousin hated it, and I fell in love with it, and I ended up going for eight weeks," Aberman said.

When her family relocated to Jensen Beach, Aberman joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive sailing career truly began to flourish. "That is where the sailing adventure took off for me," Aberman said. Aberman describes herself as an adrenaline junkie and says she is drawn to the sport's most challenging conditions. "When it's windy, I've always struggled to stay upright and stay out of the water," she said. Despite her modest self-assessment, Aberman has won countless tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and established herself as one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit.

Aberman learned she would represent Team USA during Spring Break when she received the life-changing email. "It was during Spring Break, I got the email. I started screaming, my parents started screaming, and we were like, 'This is not real. We're going to Europe this summer," Aberman said. To prepare for the championship, she has spent recent weeks training in Spain ahead of the competition.

Racing begins Monday at the venue in France. Aberman explained the training demands the location has required. "We plan on taking the waters Monday for racing, and it's just been a lot of recovery and a lot of time and effort out on the water, but it's definitely going to be worth it. Especially in the venue we're in," she said. The championship represents a significant milestone for the competitive sailor who developed her passion for the sport at the US Sailing Center of Martin County.

cards.headline: Martin County opens $1 million in state housing funds for mobile home repairs and storm hardening
cards.teaser: Martin County will open an online portal in August for manufactured home owners to apply for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits through expanded state SHIP funding.
cards.body:
Senate Bill 594, which took effect July 1, opens $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The change follows an investigation that exposed nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida built before current federal safety standards, leaving them unable to withstand modern storms. The investigation was prompted by an EF-3 tornado that destroyed 138 homes at Spanish Lakes Country Club Community in Fort Pierce, killing six residents.

Martin County Human Services will open an online application portal in August for eligible manufactured home owners to access state housing funds. About 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, will now help mobile and manufactured homeowners under the new law. Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services said applicants can fill out an online application or call the office to have one mailed. Stellatos noted people were requesting assistance long before the law passed and the new program will help those previously ineligible. She emphasized the funding is first come, first served, so applicants should prepare their paperwork quickly.

cards.headline: Free medical clinic in Martin County sees surge in patients after ACA subsidies expired
cards.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is treating more low-income patients who lost health insurance after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies ended in January.
cards.body:
Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is seeing increased patient demand after enhanced subsidies through the Affordable Care Act expired at the start of this year, leaving many people without health insurance or access to medical care. The clinic, which serves low-income families, has capacity to accept more patients. Only about 20 patients have turned to the clinic after losing ACA coverage, but estimates show there could be upwards of 500 people in Martin County who lost access. More than 200,000 people in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year, according to Dr. Jordan Bromberg, medical director of Volunteers in Medicine.

Bromberg said the expiration is worrisome because many health conditions that get screened for can prevent terrible outcomes if found early. To qualify for care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must earn under $39,990 per year, or under $82,500 for a family of four. The clinic provides free medical care with no strings attached. Patient Rokaya McGarry said she could no longer afford health insurance after the enhanced ACA subsidies expired and began seeing medical care as a luxury until she fell very ill and called the clinic, which took over her care within a day.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes kill four relatives
cards.teaser: Carla Alvarado of West Palm Beach launched a GoFundMe campaign for her best friend's family in Venezuela after earthquakes killed four relatives and destroyed their homes.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering if her parents survived after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week. The quakes collapsed buildings and killed four of her family members: her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife. Claudia, a volleyball player, was rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. De La Correa's uncle, a former Navy member, searched through rubble in darkness after the earthquake knocked out electricity across the area. The quakes also destroyed her parents' home and businesses, including her mother's children's clothing store inside a shopping mall that collapsed entirely.

Her best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado of West Palm Beach, launched a GoFundMe campaign aiming to raise $15,000 to support De La Correa's family. Alvarado said that as Venezuelans abroad, she felt useless in the situation because she could not help with her own hands. De La Correa said the support from friends and strangers has become a lifeline as her parents return daily to the ruins of their apartment building searching for salvageable belongings, managing to recover some clothing, photos and documents.

cards.headline: Wellington Green Mall's vacant Nordstrom could become 620-unit apartment complex
cards.teaser: Bainbridge Companies has submitted plans to convert 18 acres of the empty Nordstrom store at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex.
cards.body:
Bainbridge Companies has submitted plans to convert 18 acres of the vacant Nordstrom at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex. The existing building would be demolished if the project is approved. According to Village Manager Jim Barnes, the development would include one-, two- and three-bedroom units along with three towers and a parking structure. Barnes said the project addresses a housing shortage not only in the county but throughout the state and beyond.

Some residents oppose the proposal. Richard Meyers, who has lived in Wellington for more than a decade, said he opposes adding more apartments to the area, noting there are already apartment complexes around the mall. Other residents raised concerns about traffic impact, with Gaby Martinez saying the added density could strain local roads and create bottlenecks. Barnes suggested that new development nearby could benefit the retailers that remain at the mall, noting that Macy's, Dillard's and JCPenney are high-performing stores. He added that the Macy's at the Mall at Wellington Green is the highest-performing store in the state. No timeline or cost estimate for the project has been announced, and the plans have not been approved.

hero.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle nesting season programs through September
hero.teaser: The center is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season, including guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program and Hatchling Releases.
hero.body:
Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering a variety of educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season this summer. The center said guests can participate in seasonal experiences through September, including guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. The programs are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn more about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches.

The center's Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations during the programs may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment. Loggerhead Marinelife Center also said its education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success.

Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups continue encouraging beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

cards.headline: North Palm Beach hosts Fourth of July fireworks, pool party and America 250 celebration Friday
cards.body:
North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day on July 4 with a full day of family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse. This year's event also recognizes America's 250th anniversary, bringing an added sense of celebration to the annual holiday tradition in Palm Beach County. The free community event includes a pool party, lawn games, live music, a barbecue buffet and a fireworks display scheduled for 9 p.m.

The festivities begin with a community pool party from 11 a.m. at the country club pool area. Guests can enjoy a water slide, DJ entertainment, games and activities, food and beverages, and a poolside satellite bar. Beginning at 4:30 p.m., families can participate in cornhole, Connect 4, Giant Jenga, face painting and lawn games. Live music from Solstice Reign is expected to begin around 6 p.m. The Clubhouse will host a Fourth of July barbecue buffet also starting at 4:30 p.m. Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, said the golf course will offer one of the best locations to watch the fireworks display.

hero.headline: Florida law requiring heart screenings for high school athletes takes effect statewide
hero.body:
A new Florida law mandating heart screenings for high school student athletes went into effect July 1, fulfilling a commitment born from tragedy in Port St. Joe. The Second Chance Act requires all high school student athletes to receive a medical evaluation that includes an electrocardiogram, commonly known as an EKG, before participating in school-sanctioned sports. The legislation, HB 1135, was sponsored by Rep. Jason Shoaf in the House and carried by Sen. Corey Simon in the Senate during the 2025 Legislative Session. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the measure last summer. The law honors Chance Gainer, a standout athlete at Port St. Joe High School who collapsed and died from sudden cardiac arrest during a rivalry football game.

Sudden cardiac arrest represents the leading cause of death among student athletes, accounting for approximately 75 percent of all student athlete deaths. According to research, roughly 1 in every 300 students may have an undiagnosed heart condition with the potential to be life-threatening. For 80 percent of these students, cardiac arrest serves as the first symptom. Implementing EKG screenings allows medical professionals to identify these conditions before they become fatal. Chance Gainer's parents, Equila and JJ, channeled their grief into advocating for the law's passage. "Today marks more than just the start of a new law, it marks a promise kept," Shoaf said, emphasizing that the legislation represents "a promise to every parent in Florida that we will do our best to protect their children."

PanCare of Florida has partnered with Who We Play For to provide free sports physicals and heart screenings to student athletes throughout the region. Evan Ernst, Founder and CEO of Who We Play For, stressed the importance of the measure. "The Second Chance Act represents the state-wide commitment we need to make these heart screenings accessible to every student athlete in our state," Ernst said. He added that the organization operates under the principle that no family should experience the tragedies the Gainer family endured, particularly when such outcomes could be prevented through proper precautionary measures.

As fall practice seasons approach, families should prioritize scheduling their child's required sports physical immediately. Information regarding free EKG screening events is available through the partnering organizations. The law's implementation ensures that student athletes across Florida will have access to potentially lifesaving cardiac evaluations before they compete in school-sanctioned sports.

cards.headline: Incoming Florida legislative leaders endorse three Cabinet members in fall elections
cards.teaser: Senate President-designate Jim Boyd and House Speaker-designate Sam Garrison are backing CFO Blaise Ingoglia, Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson and Attorney General James Uthmeier for re-election.
cards.body:
Senate President-designate Jim Boyd and House Speaker-designate Sam Garrison jointly endorsed three Florida Cabinet members on the ballot this year: CFO Blaise Ingoglia, Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson and Attorney General James Uthmeier. Simpson is seeking re-election, while Ingoglia and Uthmeier are running to keep posts they took by appointment last year. Boyd praised Ingoglia's "take-no-prisoners" approach to government accountability, particularly his ongoing audits of local government spending and reimbursement of localities for immigration-enforcement work. Garrison, who served alongside Ingoglia in the Legislature, described him as a "straight-talking, no-nonsense steward of the taxpayer's dollar" and cited his record in identifying fraud, waste and abuse at state and local levels.

On Simpson, who served as Senate President from 2020 to 2022, Boyd highlighted his record on national security, private property rights, conservation of natural resources and maintaining a safe food supply. A longtime egg farmer, Simpson carries support from Florida FarmPAC, the Florida Cattlemen's Association and Florida Nursery, Growers and Landscape Association. Regarding Uthmeier, Boyd called him "a proven leader who will not only keep our communities safe, but defend our freedoms," while Garrison, a former prosecutor, emphasized the importance of having a "strong, supportive, and proactive leader" in the Office of Attorney General. Uthmeier has support from the Florida Police Benevolent Association and the Florida GOP.

cards.headline: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appoints Florida Board of Governors member to reorganized federal advisory panel
cards.teaser: Ken Jones, founder of Keyhole Partners and a member of the Florida Board of Governors, will serve on the Defense Advisory Committee under a total reorganization announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
cards.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a reorganized Defense Advisory Committee that includes Florida investment leader Ken Jones among 13 new members. The panel, first established in 1985, provides independent strategic advice and recommendations to the Defense Department's Secretary and Undersecretary of Policy. Former U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer will chair the committee, with former U.S. Senator Norm Coleman, a Minnesota Republican, serving as Vice Chair. The membership also includes Netscape founder Marc Andreesen.

Jones currently sits on the Florida Board of Governors, which oversees the State University System. He is the founder and Chair of Keyhole Partners, a global investment firm, and founder and managing partner of Third Lake Partners and TL Capital, which focus on alternative investments. He previously founded Fairbourne Properties, a Chicago-based commercial real estate firm. Jones served as chief counsel and Deputy Chief of Staff from 2003 to 2007 to U.S. Senator Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican and former Senate Majority Leader, and to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee. He practiced law in Washington as Deputy General Counsel for the Republican National Committee from 1999 to 2001, working on national security and intelligence issues following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. "It's an honor to serve the administration in this capacity and to be offered the opportunity to serve alongside such a talented and distinguished group of American patriots," Jones said.

cards.headline: Democrat Alex Vindman campaign sees path to victory in Florida Senate race against Ashley Moody
cards.teaser: A strategy memo from the Vindman campaign points to polling showing President Donald Trump significantly underwater in Florida and argues the state political environment has turned sharply against Republicans.
cards.body:
Democrat Alex Vindman's campaign released a strategy memo arguing a competitive Senate race in Florida is on the table for the first time in a decade. Campaign Manager Blakely Wall said the state political environment has turned sharply against Republicans, the candidate is already performing at the Democratic ceiling before meaningful spending, and the incumbent is undefined and untested. The memo compares the current environment to 2018, when Republican Rick Scott unseated sitting Democratic U.S. Senator Bill Nelson. A Global Strategy Group survey conducted in May shows only 40 percent of Florida voters have a favorable view of congressional Republicans, while 50 percent view them unfavorably. The same polling shows incumbent U.S. Senator Ashley Moody leading Vindman 46 percent to 43 percent. However, when voters learned about Vindman's background, he took a 47 percent to 45 percent lead.

The campaign argues Moody is the weakest Republican to run for Senate in the last 25 years. Fewer than half of voters can identify Ashley Moody, and on job performance she is 28 percent positive and 28 percent negative, with 44 percent unable to rate her at all. Moody was appointed to her seat by Gov. Ron DeSantis in January 2025 and has never won it in an election. The memo also points to a shift among Hispanic voters in South Florida, noting that among Florida Hispanics, 51 percent now disapprove of Trump, and 20 percent of his 2024 Hispanic voters say they would not vote for him again.

cards.headline: Florida AFL-CIO endorses Pia Dandiya for Congress in swing district CD 22
cards.teaser: The Florida AFL-CIO, representing more than 500,000 active and retired workers, endorsed Democrat Pia Dandiya for Florida's 22nd Congressional District, citing her commitment to workers' rights and fair wages.
cards.body:
The Florida AFL-CIO, which represents more than 500,000 active and retired workers, endorsed Democrat Pia Dandiya for Florida's 22nd Congressional District. Rich Templin, the organization's Director of Politics and Public Policy, said Dandiya understands that Florida's economy is strongest when working people have a seat at the table. He cited her commitment to creating good-paying jobs, defending Social Security and Medicare, investing in infrastructure and public services, and protecting the right to organize. Dandiya, a first-generation American, former high school principal, White House Fellow and Apple strategy manager, shifted her campaign to CD 22 in May after the new congressional map took effect.

The endorsement adds to a substantial coalition backing Dandiya, which includes U.S. Representatives Lois Frankel and Jill Tokuda, Florida Senate Democratic Leader Lori Berman, and numerous state senators and local officials. She has raised more than $1.57 million from more than 12,000 individual donors across all 50 states. CD 22 runs nearly coast to coast from Marco Island in Southwest Florida to western portions of Palm Beach and Broward counties. The district has no incumbent after Democratic U.S. Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz opted to run in Florida's 20th Congressional District. About 54.6 percent of voters in new CD 22 supported Trump in 2024, though more than 51 percent voted for Joe Biden in 2020, making it a swing seat. The primary is August 18, followed by the general election in November.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch selects developer for Tropicana Field redevelopment despite City Council opposition
cards.teaser: Mayor Ken Welch formally announced his intent to sell Historic Gas Plant District land to Blake Investment Partners for an estimated $8 billion redevelopment, moving forward despite the City Council voting to call on him to slow the selection process.
cards.body:
St. Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch formally announced his intent to sell Historic Gas Plant District land to Blake Investment Partners for redevelopment of the 86-acre property around Tropicana Field. The Burg Bid proposal, led by developer Thompson Whitney Blake, will cover about 58 acres of the property, while the Pinellas County Housing Authority will develop affordable senior housing on the Third Avenue South parcel. The area was previously home to a predominantly Black neighborhood razed decades ago to make way for the ballpark. Welch described the selection as a turning point after the Tampa Bay Rays walked away from a previous stadium deal.

The Burg Bid proposal includes an estimated $8 billion redevelopment plan and about 3,600 affordable and workforce housing units, though city reviewers previously noted that much of the housing component is reserved for the second phase of the project. Evaluators highlighted the development team's track record and described the proposal's three five-year phases as more compressed than some competing visions for the site. Welch's decision directly opposes the St. Petersburg City Council, which previously voted to call on him to slow the selection process. Welch is seeking another term while facing candidates including former Gov. Charlie Crist, City Council Member Brandi Gabbard, former St. Pete Fire Chief Jim Large, community advocate Maria Scruggs and former Shore Acres Neighborhood Civic Association President Kevin Batdorf. Welch said the city will now enter negotiations and ultimately bring agreements to the City Council for approval.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis reappoints three members to Valencia College Board of Trustees
cards.teaser: Universal Orlando Chief Financial Officer Tracey Stockwell, Blair Bradley and Sean Milligan were reappointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to the Valencia College Board of Trustees, according to a news release from the Governor's Office.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis reappointed three people to the Valencia College Board of Trustees: Universal Orlando Chief Financial Officer Tracey Stockwell, Blair Bradley and Sean Milligan. According to the Governor's Office news release, Stockwell has served as Treasurer of the Universal Orlando Foundation and as a member of the Orlando Economic Partnership Executive Committee. She earned her bachelor's degree from the University of Windsor. Milligan is President of Gatlin Mill, a supply chain design company, and previously served as Vice President of GWSI, Inc., Senior Director of Supply Chain Operations for GXO Logistics, Inc., and Director of Supply Chain Solutions for Hillebrand. He earned his bachelor's degree in business administration and global logistics from the College of Charleston. Bradley is a former analyst for North American Reserve, an environmental, geologic and mining consulting company.

Bradley serves as a STEM tutor and volunteer for the local Parent Teacher Association and an alumni interviewer for the Rice Alumni Volunteer Association. She earned her bachelor's degree in biomedical engineering and managerial studies from Rice University. In 2021, Bradley gave $160 to the Empower Parents PAC, which previously was the Friends of Ron DeSantis committee, according to state records. The Florida Senate must confirm DeSantis' appointments. Valencia College has enrollment of about 75,000 students who take classes online or at the school's Orange and Osceola campuses.

hero.headline: Palm City Yacht Club installing new docking system
hero.body:
Palm City Yacht Club is implementing a new docking system at its marina facility. The yacht club, located in Martin County, is upgrading its docking infrastructure.

The installation represents a modernization effort for the Palm City facility. The yacht club serves boaters in the Martin County area along the St. Lucie River.

The new docking system will replace existing marina infrastructure at the yacht club. Palm City sits along the St. Lucie River between Stuart and the northern border of Martin County.

The yacht club has not announced a completion date for the docking system installation. Marina Dock Age reported the project on Thursday morning.

cards.headline: Two boaters rescued after vessel sinks in St. Lucie County Intracoastal Waterway
cards.teaser: Marine deputies pulled two people from the water after their boat sank on Tuesday. Both wore life jackets and escaped without injury.
cards.body:
Two boaters were rescued after their small motorized boat took on water and sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on July 1. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit responded to reports of the vessel becoming submerged, with body-worn camera footage capturing the rescue as it unfolded. Both occupants ended up in the water when their boat went down, but deputies located them quickly and found they were wearing life jackets that kept them afloat while help arrived.

Marine Unit deputies safely brought both boaters aboard their patrol vessel and transported them back to the boat ramp. Neither person reported any injuries from the incident. The sheriff's office emphasized the importance of the life-saving decision to wear life jackets, stating in a Facebook post that the incident "serves as an important reminder that wearing a life jacket can save your life." The office also noted it was "grateful this call ended safely and proud of the swift response by our Marine Unit deputies who are always ready to answer the call."

cards.headline: Fourth of July driving deaths spike 44 percent as rideshare demand surges
cards.teaser: Last Fourth of July killed 579 people nationwide in car crashes, with nearly 4 in 10 deaths involving impaired driving. Rideshare apps are seeing surge demand this weekend.
cards.body:
The Fourth of July ranks as one of America's most dangerous holidays for drivers. Last Fourth of July, 579 people died in car crashes nationwide, with nearly 4 in 10 of those deaths involving impaired driving. That rate is significantly higher than the typical 30 percent rate seen throughout the year. Historical data shows deadly crashes spike by 44 percent on Independence Day. Teenagers make up about 10 percent of these holiday fatalities, according to federal statistics.

Rideshare apps like Uber and Lyft are experiencing surge demand as celebrants use them as designated drivers. Local residents in downtown West Palm Beach are already making smart choices for the holiday. Scott said he will have a designated truck driver drop off and pick up his group for paddle boarding. Pamela plans to take an Uber to celebrate. Carlos emphasized the importance of having fun while getting home safely.

cards.headline: Delray Beach bills Palm Beach County residents thousands in retroactive sewer fees
cards.teaser: Homeowners along Franwood Drive received notices demanding back payments after a city audit. Some bills exceed $4,000 for up to three years of charges.
cards.body:
Homeowners in an unincorporated Palm Beach County neighborhood received unexpected bills for years of unpaid sewer fees from the city of Delray Beach, with some totaling more than $4,000. Several residents along Franwood Drive received notices demanding back payments after a recent audit covering up to three years of charges, along with new monthly sewer fees going forward. Candace Etzler received a notice for $3,139 and said at least a dozen homeowners in the neighborhood received similar notices. Ruth Stephens said her total was $4,494.92. The situation dates back to 1998, when nearby development disrupted septic systems and state law required residents to connect to the closest municipal sewer system.

The city completed an audit in April 2026, which triggered the retroactive billing. City Commissioner Juli Casale defended the charges, stating that when a sewer connection is identified, the city's responsibility is to determine what costs were incurred and recover the applicable fees to ensure public utility costs are paid by those receiving the service rather than being shifted to taxpayers. County Commissioner Marci Woodward said she has been in touch with the county attorney, who will be looking into the legality of the back charges and monthly payments going forward. Some residents have already paid the fees or enrolled in payment plans, fearing service disconnection.

cards.headline: Exit signs on I-95 now show Donald J. Trump International Airport
cards.teaser: Palm Beach International Airport has begun transitioning to its new name. Crews changed Exit 69B on I-95 North to read President Donald Trump International Airport.
cards.body: Palm Beach International Airport has begun the process of becoming Donald J. Trump International Airport, with the official name change set to take effect July 9. Crews were seen on I-95 North Thursday morning changing Exit 69B to President Donald Trump International Airport. cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Marine Unit rescues two boaters after vessel sinks in Intracoastal Waterway
cards.teaser: Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on Tuesday, thanks to a quick response from St.
cards.body:
Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on Tuesday, thanks to a quick response from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit and their decision to wear life jackets. The marine deputies responded to reports of a small motorized boat taking on water and becoming submerged on July 1. Body-worn camera footage captured the rescue as it unfolded.

Both occupants ended up in the water when their boat went down, but deputies say they were wearing life jackets that kept them afloat while help arrived. Marine Unit deputies quickly located the pair in the water and safely brought them aboard their patrol vessel. The boaters were then transported back to the boat ramp without any injuries reported. "This incident serves as an important reminder that wearing a life jacket can save your life," the sheriff's office said in a Facebook post. "We're grateful this call ended safely and proud of the swift response by our Marine Unit deputies who are always ready to answer the call."
